case_info.explanation: A. Determine this endometrial cancer is ofPOLE-mutated subtype. In 2013, The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) project identified 4 molecular subtypes of endometrial cancer, each with distinct clinical outcomes.1Groupings closely approximating the original TGCA subtypes can be pragmatically identified using immunohistochemistry (IHC) for MMR and p53, and next-generation sequencing for evaluation ofPOLE. The World Health Organization and FIGO 2023 staging system have endorsed this classifier, and the 4 subtypes are referred to asPOLEmutated, MMR deficient, p53 abnormal, and no specific molecular profile.2,3﻿POLE-mutated tumors (5%-10% of all endometrial cancers) are defined by the presence of pathogenicPOLEmutations, of which 11 have been currently established (Box).4These occur in the exonuclease domain and have been proven to generate the characteristic ultramutated phenotype of this subgroup and confer a favorable outcome, in part because of the known robust intratumoral T-cell response caused by an enrichment of antigenic neopeptides.5Although these neoplasms do demonstrate some relatively characteristic histological changes (often high grade in appearance and with subclonal or diffuse MMR and/or p53 IHC abnormalities indicative of secondary/resultant mutations), they cannot be reliably identified by pathological examination alone,6and Sanger or next-generation sequencing of thePOLEexonuclease domain is required for this purpose. Molecular classification of endometrial cancer is widely accepted as the standard of care in the diagnosis and management of this disease, and knowledge ofPOLEmutation status is critically important because the presence of a pathogenic mutation is thought to modify the importance of certain histopathologic and immunohistochemical findings (eg, histotype/tumor grade, abnormal expression patterns of p53). This case is an example of a tumor with underlying pathogenicPOLEmutation as well as subclonal abnormal p53 immunoexpression. When more than 1 classifying feature is seen in a tumor, the neoplasm is known as a multiple classifier. Approximately 3% to 11% of all endometrial cancers are multiple classifiers. A previous study revealed that tumors with pathogenicPOLEmutations in addition to MMR and/or p53 IHC abnormalities mostly cluster with single classifierPOLE-mutated tumors when evaluated by hierarchical clustering of TCGA endometrial cancers, based on single nucleotide variant type and somatic copy number alterations.7In addition, evidence to date suggests that multiple classifierPOLE-driven tumors also exhibit favorable clinical behavior.7-9As such, any tumor harboring a pathogenicPOLEmutation—regardless of abnormalities with MMR or p53 IHC staining, which in isolation may predict more aggressive behavior—should be classified asPOLEmutated.7 Because of the identification of an underlying pathogenicPOLEmutation in the tumor, this patient was offered and consented to participation in the international EN10/RAINBO (Refining Adjuvant Treatment in Endometrial Cancer Based on Molecular Features) BLUE trial evaluating de-escalation of adjuvant treatment inPOLE-mutated endometrial cancer.

In 2013, The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) project identified 4 molecular subtypes of endometrial cancer, each with distinct clinical outcomes.1Groupings closely approximating the original TGCA subtypes can be pragmatically identified using immunohistochemistry (IHC) for MMR and p53, and next-generation sequencing for evaluation ofPOLE. The World Health Organization and FIGO 2023 staging system have endorsed this classifier, and the 4 subtypes are referred to asPOLEmutated, MMR deficient, p53 abnormal, and no specific molecular profile.2,3﻿POLE-mutated tumors (5%-10% of all endometrial cancers) are defined by the presence of pathogenicPOLEmutations, of which 11 have been currently established (Box).4These occur in the exonuclease domain and have been proven to generate the characteristic ultramutated phenotype of this subgroup and confer a favorable outcome, in part because of the known robust intratumoral T-cell response caused by an enrichment of antigenic neopeptides.5Although these neoplasms do demonstrate some relatively characteristic histological changes (often high grade in appearance and with subclonal or diffuse MMR and/or p53 IHC abnormalities indicative of secondary/resultant mutations), they cannot be reliably identified by pathological examination alone,6and Sanger or next-generation sequencing of thePOLEexonuclease domain is required for this purpose. Molecular classification of endometrial cancer is widely accepted as the standard of care in the diagnosis and management of this disease, and knowledge ofPOLEmutation status is critically important because the presence of a pathogenic mutation is thought to modify the importance of certain histopathologic and immunohistochemical findings (eg, histotype/tumor grade, abnormal expression patterns of p53). This case is an example of a tumor with underlying pathogenicPOLEmutation as well as subclonal abnormal p53 immunoexpression. When more than 1 classifying feature is seen in a tumor, the neoplasm is known as a multiple classifier. Approximately 3% to 11% of all endometrial cancers are multiple classifiers. case_info.explanation: A. Determine this endometrial cancer is ofPOLE-mutated subtype. In 2013, The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) project identified 4 molecular subtypes of endometrial cancer, each with distinct clinical outcomes.1Groupings closely approximating the original TGCA subtypes can be pragmatically identified using immunohistochemistry (IHC) for MMR and p53, and next-generation sequencing for evaluation ofPOLE. The World Health Organization and FIGO 2023 staging system have endorsed this classifier, and the 4 subtypes are referred to asPOLEmutated, MMR deficient, p53 abnormal, and no specific molecular profile.2,3﻿POLE-mutated tumors (5%-10% of all endometrial cancers) are defined by the presence of pathogenicPOLEmutations, of which 11 have been currently established (Box).4These occur in the exonuclease domain and have been proven to generate the characteristic ultramutated phenotype of this subgroup and confer a favorable outcome, in part because of the known robust intratumoral T-cell response caused by an enrichment of antigenic neopeptides.5Although these neoplasms do demonstrate some relatively characteristic histological changes (often high grade in appearance and with subclonal or diffuse MMR and/or p53 IHC abnormalities indicative of secondary/resultant mutations), they cannot be reliably identified by pathological examination alone,6and Sanger or next-generation sequencing of thePOLEexonuclease domain is required for this purpose. Molecular classification of endometrial cancer is widely accepted as the standard of care in the diagnosis and management of this disease, and knowledge ofPOLEmutation status is critically important because the presence of a pathogenic mutation is thought to modify the importance of certain histopathologic and immunohistochemical findings (eg, histotype/tumor grade, abnormal expression patterns of p53). This case is an example of a tumor with underlying pathogenicPOLEmutation as well as subclonal abnormal p53 immunoexpression. When more than 1 classifying feature is seen in a tumor, the neoplasm is known as a multiple classifier. Approximately 3% to 11% of all endometrial cancers are multiple classifiers. A previous study revealed that tumors with pathogenicPOLEmutations in addition to MMR and/or p53 IHC abnormalities mostly cluster with single classifierPOLE-mutated tumors when evaluated by hierarchical clustering of TCGA endometrial cancers, based on single nucleotide variant type and somatic copy number alterations.7In addition, evidence to date suggests that multiple classifierPOLE-driven tumors also exhibit favorable clinical behavior.7-9As such, any tumor harboring a pathogenicPOLEmutation—regardless of abnormalities with MMR or p53 IHC staining, which in isolation may predict more aggressive behavior—should be classified asPOLEmutated.7 Because of the identification of an underlying pathogenicPOLEmutation in the tumor, this patient was offered and consented to participation in the international EN10/RAINBO (Refining Adjuvant Treatment in Endometrial Cancer Based on Molecular Features) BLUE trial evaluating de-escalation of adjuvant treatment inPOLE-mutated endometrial cancer.
